transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 mins
Attendees: Liam Patel (Redwood AE), Sana Desai (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (CatalystX CTO), Priya Rao (CatalystX ML Eng), Ethan Brooks (CatalystX SecOps)

Summary: quick discovery to understand CatalystX's current usage on OpenAI, feasibility of moving to Redwood Dedicated, concerns around eval parity (quality), runtime compatibility with vLLM/TGI, and enterprise security (VPC, KMS). Agreed to share benchmarks and schedule a tech deep dive.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Liam: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. i'm liam with redwood, account exec. sana here is our systems engineer, she'll cover the technical bits. could you do quick intros?
[00:06] Jordan: yeah hey i'm jordan, cto at catalystx. we run most inference on openai right now, about 1.2B tokens a month, mix of chat and batch embeddings.
[00:12] Priya: priya, ml eng, i own the model infra side — we use vllm on prem for some lower latency endpoints and T G I for experimentation.
[00:17] Ethan: ethan, security ops — i'll be looking at compliance, sso, k m s, that kind of thing.
[00:21] Sana: great. quick agenda: 1) current stack and pain points, 2) migration constraints (compat, eval parity), 3) security/SLA questions, 4) next steps. sound good?
[00:27] Jordan: yep go for it.

[05:02] Priya: high level pain — cost variability with openai at scale, and when we tried to self-host vllm we ran into poor tail latency on chat workloads, it spikes during burst. also consistency — outputs across providers vary so our eval metrics drift.
[05:18] Liam: yep that's common. when you say vllm tail latency, is that single-host or multi-node?
[05:23] Priya: single-host with model sharding right now, we tried multi-node but grpc overhead killed gains. also, T G I-based inference has been easier for devs but doesn't map 1:1 to openai api behaviors.

[08:40] Sana: a couple of things we focus on at redwood: continuous batching and k v cache management to keep tail latency down, and kernel selection to optimize per-sequence-length. on dedicated we can pin model variants, and you get predictable throughput.
[08:56] Priya: curious — how do you handle vllm hooks? our current tooling uses vllm callback pipeline and some custom K V caching.
[09:10] Sana: we don't rely on vllm internals; instead redwood runtime exposes api-compatible endpoints. for tooling, we offer migration helpers — e.g., our adapter handles kv cache priming and prefix caching to keep warm starts fast. for vllm/T G I parity, we have a checklist we share.

[12:34] Jordan: major blocker is eval parity. our acceptance tests expect < 2% drop on rouge/bleu and some semantic similarity scores. when we tried anthopic — anthropic? — the outputs were different enough to fail gating.
[12:46] Liam: totally. we usually recommend running side-by-side evals with your test set, and we provide a compatibility mode and model variants tuned for parity. can you describe your eval set and pass/fail thresholds?
[12:58] Priya: sure, it's a mix: 10k prompts across chat system messages, few-shot in-context examples, and 2k longer-doc summarization cases. thresholds: <2% drop in rougeL, and embeddings cosine > 0.9 for sem sim.

[16:15] Sana: that's a pretty thorough suite. we can run a benchmark on dedicated with your sample dataset; our SE team will instrument the same prompts to compare tokenization, sampling seeds, temperature handling. small note: some differences come from model release or sampling defaults; we can align those.
[16:34] Ethan: from security side, we need SOC 2 plus SSO (Okta), customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM), audit logs, and VPC peering. any red flags?
[16:44] Liam: Redwood Dedicated supports VPC private deployment, KMS integration, and audit logs. we'll share SOC2 cert and our security pack. SLA-wise, dedicated can be committed with uptime and latency SLOs.

[20:05] Priya: can you share specifics on how KMS works? we are strict about key access and HSM-backed KMS for model encryption at rest.
[20:14] Sana: yes, for private deployments we support customer-managed keys via cloud KMS (and HSM options where supported). the control plane can be customer-hosted in VPC and logs pushed to your SIEM. i'll include an architecture diagram.

[23:10] Jordan: also, what's the migration path? we have a lot of production traffic tied to openai apis and some business logic that depends on specific response shapes.
[23:22] Liam: we advise doing a canary: mirror traffic to redwood dedicated, run A/B with rollout policies, and use automatic fallback to openai if quality drops. for api compatibility, our hosted endpoints mimic openai shapes for completion and chat, though function calling semantics may require slight adapter changes.

[26:44] Priya: one technical worry: we've built tooling around T G I batching and custom tensor pipelines. will moving to dedicated require rewriting those pipelines?
[26:53] Sana: you can keep T G I for experimentation, but for production on dedicated we'd recommend using the Redwood runtime for the high-throughput endpoints — it has optimized kernels and batching; we provide SDKs and a migration adapter so the impact is minimal. also we provide sample scripts to port T G I request patterns.

[30:00] Ethan: latency numbers — we need 95th percentile < 300ms for short chat interactions (<128 tokens). can you hit that?
[30:08] Sana: with dedicated pools and proper batching we regularly achieve <200ms 95p on optimized models for that seq len. depends on model size and quantization; we can propose a profile.

[33:15] Jordan: cost — what order-of-magnitude savings vs openai? we have irregular usage but often heavy on embeddings which is expensive.
[33:24] Liam: generally customers at your scale see 3x-6x cost savings on per-token inference for embeddings and chat once on dedicated and using batching/caching; exact depends on model and commit level. we'll run a cost model if you share token histogram.

[36:00] Priya: about eval parity again — if we see a small regression in rouge but better latency/cost, what's acceptable? our product team wants quality to be at least identical for launch.
[36:10] Liam: we recommend a staged roll-out: internal canary, then a controlled beta with selective user segments. if quality delta exists, we can try alternate model variants, quantization profiles, and sampling param alignment. we also have a rollback policy to openai endpoints.

[38:45] Sana: quick note on telemetry: our console provides token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and per-model traces. you can tie quality regression alerts to your eval sets so we detect shifts early.

[41:12] Jordan: ok sounds good. next steps — send pricing, security docs, and benchmark checklist. schedule deep technical session with infra.
[41:22] Liam: agreed. i'll send pricing and contract templates. sana will send the benchmark guide and runbook. priya will upload sample evals. ethan will confirm security gating items.
[41:31] Ethan: noted. Okta is our SSO, we'll include SCIM details.

[44:00] Liam: thanks all. we'll follow up with the items — expect emails in next 48 hours.
[44:06] Jordan: thanks everyone. bye.

--- End transcript ---
